text.p: Copenhagen Airports on Thursday reported a rise in 1996 net profits that was well below market expectations but said it was satisfied with its 12-13 percent growth and recommended a rise in the dividend.

The company declared full-year net profit of 279 million crowns, 13 percent up from 1995's 247 million but short of analysts' average forecast of 298 million or even the most pessimistic estimate of 290 million.
The report also showed a 12 percent rise in pre-tax profits to 422 million crowns from 376 million in 1995.
It said that the results were "satisfactory" noting a seven percent rise in passenger traffic to around 16.1 million and a 12 percent increase in operations to 270,431.

The company, which operates Copenhagen International Airport and a small airfield west of the capital, said that a rise in costs to 674 million crowns in 1996 from the previous year's 560 million trimmed the result.

"The rise in costs is attributable to generally increased activity, the current extension work on the (international) airport and special items including an environmental study, upgrade of computer systems and marketing," a statement said.
Copenhagen airport is engaged in a 10-year, seven billion crown investment programme to accommodate major changes over the next three years or so.
It expects a bridge and tunnel link between Copenhagen and the nearby Swedish city of Malmo to boost airport passenger traffic to about 20 million when it opens in the year 2,000.
The tunnel entrance on the Danish side is close to the airport which will benefit from new motorway and train connections as part of the link project.
The airport is building a rail terminal and a new pier with five gates.
It will also have to introduce segregated passenger zones when the Schengen European passport-free zone embraces the Nordic countries in 1999 or 2000.

It said that revenue from airport shopping could well fall when duty free sales to those travelling within the European Union end in 1999, although it would be counteracted to some extent by higher airport taxes.
Airport improvements meant continued rising costs, it added.
"In view of the above it is the company's expectation that in 1997 we can expect stable profit growth on the level of the growth between 1995 and 1996," it said.

The balance of good and bad news in the report was reflected in the company share's movements. After swinging between 674 crowns and 690 it had settled by mid-afternoon at 685 -- unchanged from Wednesday's close.
Copenhagen Airport, 51.3 percent state-owned, recommended an increase in the 1996 dividend to 7.5 percent from 1995's 7.0 percent.
About 60 percent of flight operations in and out of Copenhagen International Airport are carried out by Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS).
